Generation expansion planning considering health and societal
damages e A simulation-based optimization approach
Mark D. Rodgers a, *, David W. Coit b, Frank A. Felder c, Annmarie Carlton d
a Rutgers Business School, Department of Supply Chain Management, Newark, NJ, USA
b Rutgers University, Department of Industrial & Systems Engineering, Piscataway, NJ, USA
c Rutgers University, Center for Energy, Economic & Environmental Policy, New Brunswick, NJ, USA
d University of California e Irvine, Department of Chemistry, Irvine, CA, USA

Keywords:
Generation expansion
Health damages
Iterative methods
Power systems planning
Simulation optimization
abstract
Electricity generation expansion planning models determine the optimal technology-capacity-
investment strategy that minimizes market costs including investment costs, and ﬁxed and variable
operating & maintenance costs over a long-term planning horizon. From a market cost perspective, fossil
fuels are among the most economical sources of electricity, and thus are the primary sources of energy
for electricity. However, these energy sources create by-products that have harmful health effects upon
exposure. In this paper, a simulation-based, metamodeling approach is leveraged to quantify health
damages associated with power grid expansion decisions by linking the outputs of generation expansion
planning simulations with a screening tool that quanti ﬁes the human health damages from the elec-
tricity sector. Using this as a surrogate function for health damages, these costs are included in the
objective function of a generation expansion planning model, in addition to market costs and the social
damages of carbon emissions and methane leakage to minimize societal damages. Applying an
improvement algorithm, candidate data points are selected to enhance metamodel prediction capability.
Finally, using an updated metamodel, a new expansion plan is found. This framework enables re-
searchers to better understand the health implications of long-term capacity expansion decisions.

1. Introduction
Fossil fuels, mainly coal and natural gas, are the primary sources
of energy for electricity in the United States, accounting for nearly
67% of electricity generation, due to the fact that they are
economical and reliable energy sources [ 1]; [ 2]; [ 3]. However,
burning fossil fuels to generate electricity produces air emissions
that contribute to smog, which can ultimately lead to heart con-
ditions, chronic lung conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, and
emphysema, and other negative health implications [ 4]. Further-
more, these health risks are magniﬁed when the weather is warmer
and sunnier, as electricity demand is highest during these periods
[5]. As a result of these health implications, additional costs are
passed onto consumers, and society at large, in the form of exter-
nalities or damages [ 4].
Greenhouse gases, which are also by-products of fossil fuels,
lead to increased global temperatures, yielding changes in precip-
itation, increased frequencies and intensities of extreme weather
events, as well as rising sea levels [ 1]; [2]; [3]. These consequences
impact human health by affecting our sources of food and water, air
quality, and exposure to extreme weather events [ 1]; [ 2]; [ 3]. The
most prevalent greenhouse gases in atmosphere are carbon dioxide
(CO2), accounting for approximately 81% of the total greenhouse
gas emissions in the United States as of 2014, and methane (CH 4),
accounting for roughly 1 1% of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in
2014 [1]; [2]; [3]. Furthermore, electricity generation accounted for
nearly 30% of all U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in 2014 e approx-
imately two-thirds of which are from burning fossil fuels [ 1]; [ 2];
[3].
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conducted a
comprehensive study to quantify the estimated societal damages,
in terms of $/metric ton of CO2, associated with its air emissions [1];
[2]; [ 3]. CH 4 is the second most prevalent greenhouse gas emitted
in the United States [ 1]; [2]; [3]. This is mainly due to leakage from
the production, processing, storage, transmission, and distribution

of natural gas, which occurs at a rate between 1% and 8% per MWh
of electricity generated [ 6]. According to the Intergovernmental
Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the 20-year global warming po-
tential (or GWP) of CH 4 is approximately 72 times that of CO 2 [7].
Aside from the global warming potential of CH 4 and its approxi-
mated leakage rate, the associated health damages have not been
studied in suf ﬁcient detail.
In the context of power systems planning and optimization, the
topic of modeling and mitigating health damages from electricity
sector air emissions is well-studied. In the short-term planning
case, the Air Pollutant Optimization Model (APOM) solves the unit
commitment model, for day-ahead dispatch, in the state of Georgia
with the assistance of a reduced-form air quality model [ 8]. The
objective function in the APOM tool is to minimize electricity
production costs and monetized health impact cost estimates. As
aligned with our research, the creators of the APOM tool recognize
that health impact costs are dif ﬁcult to quantify though deter-
ministic methods, as they have a highly non-linear relationship
with electricity generation and the associated air emissions. The
pollutants studied in this research are ozone, PM 2.5,S O 2 and NOX.
To estimate health impact costs, a baseline unit commitment model
along with the inputs and outputs of two EPA models are syn-
chronized linearly to develop regression models that predict health
impact costs as a function of decision variables in the unit
commitment model. The ﬁrst EPA model, the Community Multi-
scale Air Quality model (CMAQ), geospatially and temporally
models air pollutant concentrations in the atmosphere [ 9]. The
second EPA model, the Environmental Bene ﬁts Mapping and
Analysis Program (BenMAP), determines the economic value of the
subsequent air pollution-related illnesses and deaths [10]. To assess
the stochasticity of health impact costs, various sensitivity analyses
are executed by varying key parameters in the unit commitment
model, and assessing the results post-optimally in CMAQ and
BenMAP.
In the context of long-term planning and capacity expansion,
the most popular approach to mitigating health and other damages
from air emissions is to utilize deterministic cost penalties in the
objective function. Alves and Uturbey applied a single objective
generation expansion planning (GEP) model with aggregate dam-
age estimates of environmental impact costs in the objective
function along with the electricity generation costs to study
expansion planning decisions and the associated health damages in
Brazil [ 11]. Similar work was done by Nguyen in Vietnam, consid-
ering health damages as deterministic penalties in the objective
function of the model [ 12]. Over a 20-year planning horizon, their
models suggest major reductions in fossil fuel dispatch in favor of
signiﬁcant investments in renewable energy technologies and
other low carbon emitting technologies. Related research, consid-
ering expansion of both the generation and transmission networks,
was done in Saudi Arabia's electricity sector, [ 13].
Another common approach used to develop expansion plans
that mitigate health and other damages is multiple objective opti-
mization. Karaki et al. solve a bi-objective optimization model with
the goal of minimizing the competing objective functions of elec-
tricity generation costs and deterministic environmental impact
costs or emissions costs [ 14]. As extended by Becker et al. these
researchers solve a bi-objective GEP model by weighting each of
these objectives a portfolio of potential expansion plans is devel-
oped [15]. Selcuklu et al. further extend this work by solving a GEP
problem with the aims to minimize market costs and air pollutant
emissions (and consequently adverse health effects) simulta-
neously in a bi-objective model. Additionally, this research in-
troduces a Pareto Uncertainty Index (PUI) to understand the impact
of uncertainty in climate change projections, thus allowing the
ranking of solutions on the Pareto front based on dominance
criterion [ 16]. Gitizadeh et al. solve a multi-objective generation
expansion planning model that considers renewable investment
options and various economic and government incentive decisions.
The authors simultaneously maximize economic returns and
minimize fuel costs and carbon emissions [ 17].Chen et al. devel-
oped a bi-objective generation expansion planning model that
simultaneously minimizes total system costs and carbon emissions
in China [ 18].
Researchers have also used GEP models to study the impact of
various strategies for integrating renewable energy sources in to
the electric power grid in order to reduce emissions and mitigate
health damages. To study the impact on increased wind generation
on capacity expansion plans, Schenk and Chan formulate the GEP
model as a least-cost, mixed integer linear program with minimum
wind dispatch requirements over a 19-year planning horizon [ 19].
Farghal and Aziz extended this research by restricting technology
investments for capacity expansion to renewable sources, which
yields signiﬁcant emissions reductions, but increases market costs
[20]. Nualhong et al. consider CO
2 emissions by considering a
penalty for excessive CO 2 emissions as well as minimum invest-
ment requirements for biomass capacity [ 21]. Fell and Lin solve a
GEP with hourly dispatch decisions and stochastic parameters to
evaluate the cost effectiveness of various renewable policies, such
as renewable portfolio standards, feed-in tariffs, and production
subsidies. Additionally, they evaluate the impact of increased
penetration of wind and solar generation in Texas on electricity
prices and market dynamics [ 22]. To evaluate long-term decar-
bonization strategies for the Portuguese market, Amorim et al.
employ the Integrated MARKAL-EFOM (MARKet ALlocation-Energy
Flow Optimization Model), to ﬁne least-cost investment strategies
through 2050 [ 23]. Similar work was done by Pereira et al. in the
Portuguese market using a 10-year, mixed integer model deter-
mining optimal integration of renewable energy sources [ 24].
Seddighi and Ahmadi-Javid solve the generation expansion plan-
ning problem with transmission expansion decisions, while incor-
porating uncertainties about future, as well as potential
disruptions. Their work also considers various sustainability regu-
lations and policies that are evaluated for the Iranian market [ 25].
Koltsaklis and Georgiadis evaluate the impact of CO 2 emissions
pricing in the context of GEP by including unit commitment con-
straints into the model [ 26]. Aryanpur and Sha ﬁei investigate the
economic impact of incorporating renewable energy sources to
reduce carbon emissions in the Iranian market. Using the MESSAGE
(Model for Energy Supply Strategy Alternative and their General
Environmental Impacts) model, they evaluate various strategies,
including investment plans, carbon taxes, and government in-
centives [ 27]. The MESSAGE model was also leveraged by G. and
Aliakbarisani as a decision support tool to solve the GEP problem
considering the cost of sustainability in Iran [ 28]. Li et al. solve a
least-cost GEP model with stochastic climate change scenarios,
with capacity expansion, electricity dispatch, and capacity retire-
ment decision variables [ 29]. Using a two-stage stochastic pro-
gramming approach, Li et al. evaluate the cost-risk tradeoff
associated with integrating renewable portfolio standards over a
10-year planning horizon in the Guangdong Province of China [ 30].
Hua et al. also solve a GEP with unit commitment constraints to
evaluate operational ﬂexibility in Texas with increased renewables
penetration [31].
Based on the GEP literature, there is a vast array of material
related to mitigating health damages using multi-objective models,
emissions limits, deterministic penalties in the objective function
for air emissions, and renewable portfolio standards. However, the
literature is devoid of a method that explicitly considers human
health externalities in the objective function of a GEP model. The
primary motivation of this research is to establish a closed-form

relationship between power grid expansion decisions and the
associated health damages, in order to determine an optimal
expansion plan to mitigate health risks. In this paper, these risks are
addressed by presenting a framework to solve the long-term power
grid capacity expansion planning problem, known as generation
expansion planning (GEP). In this model, the optimal technology
capacity investment strategy that minimizes health damages from
air emissions, market costs including investment costs, and ﬁxed
and variable O &M costs of generation, as well as other societal
damages including the social cost of carbon emissions and methane
leakage is determined.
To include health damages in our model, we leverage the
framework developed by Rodgers et al., which uses a metamodel to
quantify health damages from NO X and SO 2 emissions associated
with power grid capacity expansion decisions, is leveraged [ 32,33].
In this work, health damages from simulated GEP expansion plans
are evaluated in the Co-Bene ﬁts Risk Assessment (COBRA) model.
COBRA is an EPA screening model that helps state and local gov-
ernments assess human health damages from air emissions at the
county, state, regional, or national level [ 34]. From these simula-
tions, the authors derive a closed-form relationship that approxi-
mates health damages as a function of GEP decisions. This
metamodel is included in the objective function of our model as a
surrogate for health damages.
Societal damages from CO
2 emissions are included in the
objective function by leveraging the data from EPA studies on the
social costs of CO 2 emissions [1]; [2]; [3]. Furthermore, since health
damages from CH 4 leakage have not been studied in suf ﬁcient
detail in the literature, a methane leakage rate is approximated
deterministically, and incorporated into the GEP model as an input
parameter. Finally, since a portion of the GEP objective function is a
model, an iterative procedure to conduct additional computer-
based GEP simulations to re ﬁt our metamodel and update our
GEP model solutions is presented.
The structure of the remainder of the paper is as follows. Section
2 presents the framework for developing GEP expansion plans that
minimize societal damages. Section 3 demonstrates the model with
a numerical example, using the Northeastern United States power
grid as a case study. Finally, the paper is concluded by summarizing
the main ﬁndings, as well as presenting potential research exten-
sions of this work in Section 4.
2. Model development
In this section, the simulation-based optimization framework
used to solve our GEP model is presented. The ﬂow chart in Fig. 1,
adapted from research of Han & Zhang, summarizes the steps to
create a ﬁnal expansion plan.
The ﬁrst step in this process, seed generation, generates a
diverse sample space of data points. To accomplish this, 100 market
costs minimization GEP model simulation trials are executed.
Within each trial, the following model parameters are sampled
from a normal distribution a coef ﬁcient of variation following a
uniform random variable on the interval [0,1] [ 33]:
Each of these simulation trials are then compared to a baseline
GEP model to obtain the percent change in NO X and SO2 emissions
from the baseline. For each trial, these values are used as inputs to
be evaluated in the COBRA model to quantify health damages. To
elaborate, COBRA users generate scenarios by specifying changes in
the emissions, namely NO
X and SO 2, on an annual basis for a
speciﬁed region [ 34]. The model then quanti ﬁes the associated
changes in changes in particulate matter (PM 2.5) concentrations
between a baseline scenario and an experimental (or control)
scenario. A source-receptor matrix translates the air pollution
emissions changes into changes in ambient PM 2.5. Thus, since CO-
BRA approximates changes in PM 2.5 concentrations as part of the
approximation of health damages, we do not explicitly consider
this pollutant in our model.
Using a kriging metamodel, a closed-form function that relates
changes in dispatching decisions from GEP model outputs to health
damages from NOX and SO2 emissions is developed. Using this as a
surrogate function for health damages, GEP model is solved. To
ensure the prediction accuracy of the metamodel, and conse-
quently yield better GEP model outputs, the expected improvement
of the metamodel is evaluated to determine when to terminate the
algorithm or to execute additional GEP simulations to enhance the
metamodel.

The societal damages from CO 2 emissions are approximate

distribution of natural gas are given in Equation (6) [1]; [ 2]; [ 3].

[3]. These values are denoted using bi, where i indexes the units
with natural gas fuel sources.
/C15 Step 3: Natural gas is approximately 90% methane by compo-
sition, denoted by g [3].
/C15 Step 4: The value GWP is de ﬁned as the 100-year global
warming potential (or GWP) of methane, which is 28 times that
of CO2 [36].
/C15 Step 5: Finally, per the ideal gas law, the density of methane is a
function of temperature. Based on climate change projections,
temperatures are expected to increase by approximately 4 /C14 Fb y
the year 2100 [3]. Assuming 1 atm of pressure, and prorating the
temperature growth to the time-horizon considered in our GEP
model, the density of methane is simulated by applying a uni-
form distribution to the temperature within the region of the
prorated projected boundaries. The density of methane is
denoted by by h.
/C15 Step 6: The product of a; bi; g; GWP; and h yields the approxi-
mated CH4 leakage rate, bli;e, to be used in the model.

2.2. Solution procedure
Since a portion of the objective function in this GEP model is a
surrogate function, it is necessary to ensure that the metamodel,
and thus the resulting expansion plan, is re ﬂective of the true
relationship between inputs and outputs [ 35]. In our case, we
consider the relationship between electricity generation and health
damages. The ﬁrst step in this procedure is to solve the GEP model

baseline GEP model for evaluation in the COBRA tool [ 37]. Upon
experimentation in COBRA, this collection of data points is then
appended to the original experimental data set, and the metamodel
is reﬁt. Equation (25) deﬁnes the expected improvement function,

The goal of this model is to determine the dispatch plan that
maximizes the expected improvement of the metamodel. Equation
(26) is the energy balance constraint, and Equations (27) and (28 )
are the transmission constraints, all of which are from our baseline
GEP model. The decision variables in this model are xytr1 i and

We follow the procedures outlined in this section iteratively
until we reach one of the two termination criteria:
/C15 Case 1: When the expected improvement model reaches zero,
we terminate our model. This implies that our metamodel
cannot be improved any further with more experimental data;
/C15 Case 2: From iteration to iteration, if the objective function
changes less than a pre-speci ﬁed tolerance range, we terminate
our model.

In this section, our framework is applied to a series of scenarios
to evaluate the impact of constraints and objective function costs
on GEP expansion plans. For these examples, we consider the PJM
Interconnection LLC, which is a regional transmission organization
that is part of the Eastern Interconnection grid in the Northeastern
U.S., as shown in the schematic representation in Fig. 2 .

3.1. Discussion
Using the methodology presented in Section 2 of this paper, a
multi-period, total societal cost minimization GEP problem is
formulated and solved using a simulation-based optimization
approach. In comparing the results of this approach to various
cases, the proposed method is more effective at mitigating human
health damages associated with power grid capacity expansion
decisions, than leveraging other alternatives, such as using deter-
ministic penalties in the objective function or implementing
emissions limits and renewable portfolio standards as model con-
straints. However, in order to realize the minimized health dam-
ages, increased investments in renewable energy sources must be
made, thus driving increased market costs over the planning
horizon.
While the results presented in this section are aligned with
related research on this topic, as presented in Section 1, this pre-
sents a potential feasibility challenge due to large investments in
wind technology as an energy source. The proposed wind capacity
expansions, as outlined in the Simulated Health Damages, case
would increase the total wind capacity of the network to over
33 GW by 2040. This capacity expansion, from an initial network
capacity of approximately 2 GW, translates to over 10% of the total
electricity generation in region under investigation. This is in line

pacity expansions, while much more aggressive than the expansion

required to fully assess the challenges of this investment strategy.
This research enables policy makers to make more informed
decisions on expanding power grid capacity. Since typical GEP
models do not include health damages in the objective function, the
resulting expansion plans include fossil fuel investments. While
these energy sources can economically (in terms of market costs)
and reliably satisfy the load on the system, they also produce
emissions that are potential health hazards. This research presents
a framework for decision makers to mitigate these concerns, while
understanding the resulting implications of a given capacity in-
vestment strategy.
4. Conclusions
This paper presents an optimization framework to solve the GEP
problem that minimizes total societal damages, inclusive of market
costs (investment costs, ﬁxed and variable operating & mainte-
nance costs, and fuel costs) and health and other damages associ-
ated with pollutant emissions from electricity generation via
simulation-based optimization methods. Traditional approaches
to mitigating health and other damages in the context of GEP, such
as including emissions limits and renewable portfolio standards as
model constraints or applying deterministic multipliers as pen-
alties in the objective function, are not as effective at reducing the
health effects from electricity generation in comparison to the
analytical framework presented in this research. This is the ﬁrst
comprehensive attempt at using advanced statistical and simula-
tion methods to quantify the health damages in the context of GEP.
This allows researchers and policy makers to make more informed
decisions on expanding power grid capacity.
Since the models propose signi ﬁcant investments in renewable
energy sources, this work may be extended to include elements of
intermittency and disruption in their supply. To assess this issue,
we may consider the following optimization approaches (amongst
many other potential variations): ( i) assuming the capacity factors
of these units to be stochastic parameters in our model, ( ii)
leveraging simulation to estimate the capacity factors of renewable
units, or ( iii) applying seasonality factors to the capacity factors.
Since our model proposes signi ﬁcant wind capacity expansions,
these research extensions are of major relevance, as further
research is required to fully address feasibility concerns along other
challenges associated with wind capacity expansions.
In conclusion, this research makes the following research con-
tributions: ( i) employing a kriging metamodel to express the rela-
tionship between GEP decisions and health damages, ( ii) solving a
large-scale, multi-period optimization model over an extended
time horizon with this metamodel as a surrogate objective func-
tion, and ( iii) developing an iterative procedure to resample and
reﬁt the metamodel to yield robust candidate solutions.
